title: Environmental impact of artificial intelligence
summary:
The environmental impact of artificial intelligence includes immediate impacts due to computing, impacts related to its intended use and application, and systemic effects through the societal systems that AI usage affects. Immediate impacts include substantial electricity consumption for training and the usage of deep learning models, as well as the related carbon footprint and water usage impact. One study suggested that by 2027, energy costs for AI could increase to 85-134 TWh, nearly 0.5% of all current electricity usage. The computation required to train the most advanced AI models doubles every 3.4 months on average, leading to exponential power usage.

Generative AI systems including large language models have significantly higher environmental impacts than specific AI systems. Training large language models generally requires much more electricity compared to running a single prediction on the trained model. AI data centers are materially intense, requiring a large amount of electronics that use specialized mined metals and which eventually will be disposed as e-waste. In 2024, data centres accounted for about 1.5% of the world's electricity consumption, but demand is projected to double to 945 TWh by 2030, potentially exceeding Japan's current total electricity consumption. Beyond electricity demands, a great deal of water is needed to cool the hardware used for training, deploying, and fine-tuning generative AI models.

There has been a growing divide in the scientific community over the different benefits AI can provide for environmental science and research. While potential benefits include AI-powered research for the development of carbon sequestering plants and the use of AI to make collection of ecological data faster and more streamlined, there is disagreement over whether this offsets the detrimental effects AI usage has on the environment.

The environmental impacts of AI have been a blindspot in the range of AI legislation proposed in the US Congress. The European Union intends to regulate the environmental impact of artificial intelligence on multiple levels of government through the European Green Deal. More than 190 countries have adopted a series of non-binding recommendations on the ethical use of AI, which covers the environment.
